h: Got a letter from BMI, ASCAP, SESAC or GMR?
t: The letter is real, and many venues get one. A first letter does not usually go away on its own. Here is what it means and what to do this week. Rules: United States Other countries On this page What it isThis weekWhat to avoidHelp

Some groups give businesses licenses to play songs in public. They do this on behalf of songwriters and publishers. These groups are called performing rights organizations, or PROs. Bars, restaurants and hotels are among the businesses that get these licenses (U.S. Copyright Office, “Copyright and the Music Marketplace” (2015)). ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR each represent their own members’ songs. So a venue can need more than one license (SESAC, “What is a performing rights organization?”). A first letter usually offers a license and asks about your venue. Some lead to more contact later. In October 2026, music publishers and songwriters linked to ASCAP filed lawsuits in several states. They sued hospitality and entertainment businesses for copyright infringement. Several of the complaints reportedly say there was repeated contact about licensing first (Brownstein client alert, “Music licensing under the microscope” (Nov. 9, 2026)). For each work infringed, a court may award statutory damages of $750 to $30,000. If the infringement is willful, it may award up to $150,000. If the infringer proves it was innocent, the award can be as little as $200 (17 U.S.C. §504(c), statutory damages

- Note the deadline and who sent it. Make sure it really comes from a PRO. - List every way you use music : where your background music comes from, live music, DJs, karaoke, TVs, events and social videos. - Gather what you already pay : your music service contract and any PRO bills. - Check your music service terms. Some services say their license covers the recorded music they supply. It does not cover live bands, DJs or karaoke (Pandora CloudCover, licensing FAQ). - Check the small-business exemption if you only play radio or TV (see the rules). - Reply on time, with facts. If the letter mentions a lawsuit or comes from a lawyer, talk to a licensed attorney first.

- Ignoring it. Several lawsuit complaints reportedly describe repeated contact before the lawsuit (Brownstein client alert, “Music licensing under the microscope” (Nov. 9, 2026)). Staying silent tends to make the matter last longer, not end it. - Thinking your music service covers live performances. Services usually cover their own recorded music, not live bands, DJs or karaoke (Pandora CloudCover, licensing FAQ). - Thinking one PRO license covers everything. Each PRO licenses its own members’ works. - Switching to a personal streaming account. Spotify’s terms allow only “personal, non-commercial use” (Spotify End User Agreement, section 3).

h: Why a personal account is not enough
t: The big consumer services are for personal listening only. Here is what their terms say: - Spotify gives permission for “personal, non-commercial use” (Spotify End User Agreement, section 3). - Apple allows use of its services and content “only for personal, noncommercial purposes” (Apple Media Services Terms, section F). - YouTube’s terms say you may listen for personal, non-commercial use. They also say you may not publicly screen videos or stream music from the service (YouTube Terms of Service). Playing a personal plan to your customers goes beyond those terms.

- Business music service : Published entry prices start around $15 to $25 per location per month, on yearly terms. Pandora CloudCover starts at $16.95, Mood Media at $15.30, and Rockbot is $25 per zone. Higher tiers cost more. We checked these prices on November 12, 2026; see the sources for current prices. A service generally covers its own recorded songs played in public areas. It does not cover live performances, cover artists, DJs or karaoke (Pandora CloudCover, licensing FAQ). - Direct PRO licenses : Some venues play music that a licensed service does not supply. Others host live music, DJs or karaoke. These venues may need licenses from each PRO whose songs are played (U.S. Copyright Office, “Copyright and the Music Marketplace” (2015)). A PRO (performing rights organization) is a group that licenses songs to be played in public. - Radio or TV, small venue : Some radio and TV broadcasts can be exempt in small venues. There are limits on equipment. See the rules.

h: Is my venue exempt from music licensing?
t: Possibly. But only for some radio and TV broadcasts, and only within strict limits. Rules: United States Other countries On this page The ruleNever coveredNext step

Under 17 U.S.C. §110(5)(B), a business does not need a separate license to play certain radio and TV transmissions of music. The law calls this music a “nondramatic musical work”. The transmission must come from a radio or TV station licensed by the FCC (the Federal Communications Commission). For video, it can also come from a cable system or satellite carrier. The exemption applies only if all of these hold (17 U.S.C. §110(5), exemption for certain establishments): - Food and drink venues : Under 3,750 gross square feet, not counting customer parking. No limits on equipment. - Other businesses : Under 2,000 gross square feet. No limits on equipment. - Larger venues : Sound on no more than 6 loudspeakers, with no more than 4 in any one room. Video on no more than 4 screens, with no more than 1 per room. No screen can be larger than 55 inches, measured diagonally. - In every case : There is no direct charge to see or hear the transmission. The transmission is not sent on beyond the venue. And the copyright owner has licensed the transmission.

- Streaming services, downloads, CDs or vinyl. The law covers only broadcast, cable and satellite transmissions. - Live music, DJs or karaoke. - Music you add to social media or marketing videos. This is a plain-English summary of the law, for general information. Check the current text, or ask a licensed attorney, before you rely on it. You can find an overview from the Congressional Research Service, RS21107.

h: Do I need a license for live music, DJs or karaoke?
t: Usually yes. The four music licensing groups (PROs) all say the license sits with the venue. It does not sit with the band or the DJ. Rules: United States Other countries On this page Who is responsibleYour music serviceThe DJ's subscriptionWhich licensesNext step

h: It is the venue’s job, not the band’s
t: Each of the four performing rights organizations (PROs) says the same thing. The license for performances at your venue is up to the business: - ASCAP: “the business owner is legally responsible to obtain the license”. Its FAQ adds that live music of any kind, “including DJ nights and karaoke”, needs public performance licenses (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs). - BMI: whether music is “performed by a live band, DJ or karaoke, the business owner must obtain permission from the copyright owner” (BMI Music Licensing FAQs). - SESAC: “a business cannot shift its responsibility to musicians or entertainers” (SESAC, who is responsible for paying music licensing fees). It also says: “Paying the band does not cover you” (SESAC FAQ). - GMR: the owner or operator is responsible for the performances at its venue. Paying the performers “will not relieve you of your licensing obligation” (Global Music Rights FAQ). Courts took the same view long ago. In 1929, a federal appeals court held a dance hall owner liable for songs played by a hired orchestra. That was true “even though the orchestra be employed under a contract that would ordinarily make it an independent contractor” (Dreamland Ball Room v.

h: Your background music service usually stops at background music
t: Business music services license the songs they send you for background play. Several say in writing that live shows fall outside that: - Pandora CloudCover : “A background music license also does not cover live performances, cover artists, DJs”. Also, the music cannot be a core part of the activity, as with karaoke (CloudCover licensing FAQ, updated July 2026). - Soundtrack : Soundtrack’s terms name two cases. One is a business that “Plays music from another source other than the Service such as a DJ, karaoke, or live music”. The other is one that “Charges an admission fee”. In both cases, the public performance rights “are not licensed by Soundtrack” (Soundtrack General Terms, March 2026). - Custom Channels : “Music from DJs, live bands, karaoke, or trivia events is not covered and may require separate PRO licenses” (Custom Channels help center). The PROs describe the same limit from their side. SESAC says a service’s license “only extends to the music they supply” to places with “no admission, membership or similar charge” (SESAC FAQ). ASCAP says karaoke and DJ nights need “additional licensing by the establishment” (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs).

h: The DJ’s own subscription is not your license
t: DJs often stream from a DJ service. Some of those services say plainly that the subscription does not cover playing in public: - Beatport: streamed content “is intended for your personal use only”. Public performance “will require additional licensing, which is not included as part of your subscription” (Beatport Streaming terms of use). - VirtualDJ: its Online Music membership “does not give you the right to perform music in public”. The DJ or the venue needs the licenses to play in public (VirtualDJ, Public Performance License). A clause in your booking agreement can say who handles what. But the PRO statements above put the license with the venue.

h: Which licenses a live night touches
t: A band or DJ can play songs from any catalog. Each PRO licenses only the songs it represents. So a venue that pays one or two PROs can still have gaps on live nights. Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR? explains how the four fit together. The page on what a license costs shows how live nights change the fee.

h: Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?
t: It depends on what you play. ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR are PROs (performing rights organizations). They license songs to be played in public. Each PRO licenses only its own songs, and many songs are split between several of them. Rules: United States Other countries On this page Each licenses its ownSplit songsHow they differLook up a songNext step

h: Each PRO licenses only its own songs
t: All four PROs say the same thing about their licenses: - BMI says a license from another PRO “allows you only to perform copyrighted music represented by that organization”. The reason, BMI says, is that “each PRO licenses a unique repertoire of music” (BMI Music Licensing FAQs). - SESAC says each organization “licenses only the copyrighted works of its own respective copyright holders” (SESAC FAQ). - GMR says licenses with ASCAP, BMI and SESAC “do not grant you authorization” to perform music by GMR’s writers, “and vice versa” (Global Music Rights FAQ). - ASCAP says “you need a license with each PRO that represents the creators of the music that you play” (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs). So the real question is not “which PRO is the right one”. It is “whose songs are played here, and which licenses cover them”. A curated background music service changes the answer for the music it supplies. See Can I play Spotify in my restaurant or bar?

h: One song can need more than one license
t: Songs often have several writers who belong to different PROs. The U.S. Copyright Office notes that the rights to musical works “are often split among multiple songwriters, with differing publishers and PROs” (U.S. Copyright Office, “Copyright and the Music Marketplace” (2015), p. 123). So one song can belong to more than one PRO. The Department of Justice describes the result. It is called fractional licensing. A PRO licenses only its share of a work, “meaning that a licensee must obtain a license from all of the PROs affiliated with the work (or from the songwriters or publishers directly) in order to legally perform it” (DOJ statement closing its review of the ASCAP and BMI consent decrees (January 15, 2021), p. 2). A licensee is the business that holds the license.

ASCAP and BMI work under long-standing antitrust consent decrees with the Department of Justice. SESAC and GMR do not. Antitrust law is the law on fair competition. A consent decree is an agreement approved by a court. The Copyright Office puts it this way: “neither SESAC nor GMR is subject to such direct antitrust regulation” (Copyright and the Music Marketplace, p. 34). The DOJ notes the decrees “regulate only ASCAP and BMI” (DOJ statement, January 15, 2021, p. 2). For a venue, the day-to-day point is simpler. Each PRO sets its own fees for bars and restaurants. Each one needs its own license. How much does a music license cost? explains what drives those fees.

h: Look up which PRO represents a song
t: Each PRO publishes a free search: - Songview : A shared database. BMI says it covers “the four major PROs, BMI, ASCAP, GMR and SESAC”, with ownership shares per song (Songview at BMI; also reachable from ASCAP’s repertory search). - SESAC : SESAC repertory search: titles, SESAC’s share, and its writers and publishers. - GMR : Global Music Rights search: by title, performer, songwriter or publisher. A search tells you who represents a song. It does not tell you whether your venue is licensed for it. Searching song by song is also hard to do for a live band or a DJ. They can play hundreds of songs a night.

h: How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar?
t: Each PRO charges its own fee. ASCAP and BMI base their fees mainly on your occupancy (how many people your venue can hold) and how you use music. SESAC and GMR share fewer details. Rules: United States Other countries On this page What sets the feeASCAP’s 2026 ratesBMI, SESAC and GMRThe totalNext step

The PROs look at mostly the same things: - How you use music: live, recorded, or with video. ASCAP lists “live, recorded, audio only vs. audio/visual”. It also lists the venue’s “capacity” and “how many nights a week it hosts live music” (ASCAP, why ASCAP licenses bars, restaurants and music venues). - Size. ASCAP and BMI both link their fees to occupancy. BMI says the local fire marshal most often sets this number (BMI, music licensing for bars and restaurants). - Extras on top of recorded music, such as karaoke and DJs. Any admission or cover charge counts too (ASCAP rate schedule, calendar year 2026). Where you are does not change the ASCAP rate. ASCAP says restaurants of the same size and music use pay the same, “regardless of whether the restaurant is in Oshkosh or New York City” (ASCAP).

ASCAP publishes its rates for restaurants, bars and nightclubs. The yearly fee starts with a rate per occupant (per person), made up of the lines below. That rate is multiplied by your venue’s occupancy. If there is no official occupancy, ASCAP uses the square footage divided by 20. Rates per occupant for calendar year 2026: - Live music, 4 to 7 nights a week : $8.05 - Live music, 3 nights or less : $6.70 - Recorded music, no live music : $4.69 - Recorded music, with live music : $3.10 - Enhancements: karaoke, DJs, emcees, dancing, shows, acts or games : $2.72 - Admission or cover charge : $2.72 - TV or radio only, where the broadcast exemption does not apply : $1.77 The occupancy fee is at least $502. A separate jukebox fee may apply. The schedule also adjusts for seasonal venues, and it adds an increase for inflation each year from 2027. Read the full schedule and its notes before you rely on any figure (ASCAP rate schedule and statement of operating policy, calendar year 2026).

- BMI : Says its license “starts at a little more than a dollar per day”. The fee goes up with the type of music (recorded, live, DJ, karaoke), how often it is played, and occupancy (BMI, music licensing for bars and restaurants). - SESAC : Says “music licensing fees vary by industry”. They also depend on how much music is used (SESAC, how are fees determined?). - GMR : Says rates “depend upon your type of business and how the music is presented to the public” (Global Music Rights FAQ). We found no published price list from BMI, SESAC or GMR for bars and restaurants. Ask each one for a written quote based on your occupancy and how you use music.

Each PRO licenses separately (see Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?). So your total depends on how many licenses you hold, plus any music service. The National Restaurant Association has said its members pay an average of $4,500 per year to license music (Bloomberg via Indianapolis Business Journal, July 9, 2025). That is an average across members, not a quote for any venue.

h: Music licensing glossary for venue owners
t: These are the words you will see in PRO letters, price lists and music service terms, explained in plain English. Each entry names its source and links to the page that explains it. Rules: United States Other countries Terms A to Z ABCDEFG H I J K L M N OP Q RS T U V W X Y Z SourcesNext step 20 terms, in alphabetical order. A plain-English summary for general information, not legal advice.

- ASCAP : ASCAP is one of the four groups that give businesses licenses to play songs in public. These groups are called performing rights organizations (PROs). ASCAP says “you need a license with each PRO that represents the creators of the music that you play” (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs). It publishes a list of rates for restaurants, bars and nightclubs. Fees are per occupant, which means per person your venue can hold (ASCAP rate schedule, calendar year 2026). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?; How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar?

- BMI : BMI is one of the four groups that give businesses licenses to play songs in public (PROs). BMI says a license from another PRO “allows you only to perform copyrighted music represented by that organization” (BMI Music Licensing FAQs). For bars and restaurants, BMI says its license “starts at a little more than a dollar per day”. The price goes up with the type of music, how often it is played, and occupancy (BMI, music licensing for bars and restaurants). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?; How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar? - Business music service : A business music service gives a business recorded music to play in the background, and it licenses that music. Examples are Pandora CloudCover, Mood Media, Rockbot and Soundtrack. A service usually covers its own recorded music played in public areas. It does not usually cover live performances, cover artists, DJs or karaoke (Pandora CloudCover, licensing FAQ). Explained in Can I play Spotify in my restaurant or bar?; Do I need a license for live music, DJs or karaoke?

- Consent decree : A consent decree is a set of rules that ASCAP and BMI have agreed with the Department of Justice to follow. These rules are long-standing, and they come from antitrust law, the law on fair competition. SESAC and GMR are not under them. The DOJ notes the decrees “regulate only ASCAP and BMI” (DOJ statement, January 15, 2021, p. 2). The Copyright Office says “neither SESAC nor GMR is subject to such direct antitrust regulation” (Copyright and the Music Marketplace, p. 34). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR? - Cover charge (Admission charge) : A cover charge is money a guest pays to get in, such as admission or a cover. ASCAP’s 2026 rate schedule adds a line of $2.72 per occupant for an admission or cover charge (ASCAP rate schedule, calendar year 2026). It also limits what a music service covers. Soundtrack says that if a business “Charges an admission fee”, the public performance rights “are not licensed by Soundtrack” (Soundtrack General Terms). SESAC says a service’s license “only extends to the music they supply to establishments with no admission, membership or similar charge” (SESAC FAQ). Explained in How much does a music license cost a restau

- Direct PRO license : A direct PRO license is one a venue gets from a PRO itself, not through a music service. Some venues play music that no licensed service supplies. Others host live music, DJs or karaoke. These venues may need a license from each PRO whose music is played (U.S. Copyright Office, “Copyright and the Music Marketplace” (2015)). Explained in Can I play Spotify in my restaurant or bar?

- Enhancements : Enhancements is ASCAP’s word for extras like karaoke, DJs, emcees, dancing, shows, acts or games. It is a line in ASCAP’s rate schedule. For 2026, it adds $2.72 per occupant to the yearly rate (ASCAP rate schedule, calendar year 2026). Explained in How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar?

- Fractional licensing (Split works) : Fractional licensing means each PRO can license only its own share of a song. Songs often have more than one writer, and the writers can belong to different PROs. The rights “are often split among multiple songwriters, with differing publishers and PROs” (U.S. Copyright Office, “Copyright and the Music Marketplace” (2015), p. 123). So a PRO licenses only its share of a work, “meaning that a licensee must obtain a license from all of the PROs affiliated with the work (or from the songwriters or publishers directly) in order to legally perform it” (DOJ statement, January 15, 2021, p. 2). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?

- GMR (Global Music Rights) : GMR, or Global Music Rights, is one of the four groups that give businesses licenses to play songs in public (PROs). GMR says licenses with ASCAP, BMI and SESAC “do not grant you authorization” to perform music by its writers, “and vice versa”. It also says its rates “depend upon your type of business and how the music is presented to the public” (Global Music Rights FAQ). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?; How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar?

- Live performance (Live music, DJs and karaoke) : A live performance is music played in your venue by a band, a DJ or karaoke. Each of the four PROs says the license for these shows is the business’s job, not the performer’s (ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, GMR). SESAC puts it this way: “Paying the band does not cover you” (SESAC FAQ). Business music services usually do not cover live performances (Pandora CloudCover, licensing FAQ). Explained in Do I need a license for live music, DJs or karaoke?

- Occupancy : Occupancy is how many people your venue can hold. ASCAP and BMI use this number to set their fees. BMI says the local fire marshal most often sets it (BMI, music licensing for bars and restaurants). In ASCAP’s 2026 schedule, the yearly fee is a rate per occupant times your venue’s occupancy. If there is no official occupancy, ASCAP uses the square footage divided by 20 (ASCAP rate schedule, calendar year 2026). Explained in How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar?

- Performing rights organization (PRO) : A PRO is a group that gives businesses licenses to play songs in public. It does this on behalf of songwriters and publishers. Bars, restaurants and hotels are among the businesses that get PRO licenses (U.S. Copyright Office, “Copyright and the Music Marketplace” (2015)). There are four: ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR. Each one represents its own members’ songs. So a venue can need more than one license (SESAC, “What is a performing rights organization?”). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?; Got a letter from BMI, ASCAP, SESAC or GMR? - Personal streaming account : A personal streaming account is a music plan for your own listening. Services such as Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube offer them. Their terms limit use to personal listening. Spotify allows “personal, non-commercial use” (Spotify End User Agreement, section 3). Apple allows use “only for personal, noncommercial purposes” (Apple Media Services Terms, section F). Explained in Can I play Spotify in my restaurant or bar? - PRO letter : A PRO letter is a letter from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC or GMR. A first letter usually offers a license and asks about your venue. Some lead to mor

- Repertory search (Songview) : A repertory search is a free search that shows which PRO represents a song. Each PRO publishes one. Songview is a shared database. BMI says it covers “the four major PROs, BMI, ASCAP, GMR and SESAC”, with ownership shares for each song (Songview at BMI; also reachable from ASCAP’s repertory search). SESAC and GMR publish their own searches (SESAC repertory search, Global Music Rights search). A search tells you who represents a song, not whether your venue is licensed for it. Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?

- SESAC : SESAC is one of the four groups that give businesses licenses to play songs in public (PROs). SESAC says each organization “licenses only the copyrighted works of its own respective copyright holders” (SESAC FAQ). It also says “music licensing fees vary by industry” and by how much music is used (SESAC, how are fees determined?). Explained in Do I need ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR?; How much does a music license cost a restaurant or bar? - Small-business exemption (17 U.S.C. §110(5)(B)) : The small-business exemption is a narrow rule about playing radio or TV in a business. It is found in 17 U.S.C. §110(5)(B), and it covers playing a transmission from an FCC-licensed radio or TV station (or, for video, a cable system or satellite carrier). Under US law, food and drink venues under 3,750 gross square feet, and other businesses under 2,000, have no equipment limits. Larger venues qualify only within limits on loudspeakers, screens and screen size. Other conditions apply in every case, such as no direct charge to see or hear the transmission (17 U.S.C. §110(5), exemption for certain establishments). It never covers streaming services, downloads, CDs or vinyl, live music, DJs or

- Willful infringement : Willful infringement is infringement that a court finds was willful. When a court finds this, US law allows statutory damages of up to $150,000 per work. That is above the $750 to $30,000 range that applies otherwise (17 U.S.C. §504(c), statutory damages). The range describes the law, not the likely outcome for any venue. h: Music licensing for hotels: lobby, restaurant, events and rooms
t: A hotel often uses music in many places under one roof. Here is what the music licensing groups (PROs) say about each use, in their own documents. Rules: United States Other countries On this page Music in a hotelUse by useHow fees are setNext step

h: Music in a hotel is a public performance
t: Copyright law says what it means to perform a work “publicly”. It means a performance “at a place open to the public or at any place where a substantial number of persons outside of a normal circle of a family and its social acquaintances is gathered” (17 U.S.C. §101, definitions). Put simply: a place open to the public, or a large group beyond family and friends. Groups called performing rights organizations, or PROs, license that right. They act for songwriters and publishers. SESAC puts it simply for hotels: “If your hotel uses music in guest areas, then you likely need a license” (SESAC, music licensing for hotels). SESAC lists “hotels, motels, resorts, health clubs” among its licensees (SESAC FAQ). Global Music Rights (GMR) names hotels as one of the business types it treats differently when it sets rates (Global Music Rights FAQ). Each PRO licenses only its own catalog of songs. ASCAP’s hotel license says its fees “specifically exclude the value” of rights held by “Broadcast Music, Inc., SESAC Inc. and Global Music Rights” (ASCAP Musical Works License Agreement for Hotels and Motels, 2022 form, published by AHLA). GMR says licenses from the other three “do not grant you autho

h: Hotel music uses, one by one
t: ASCAP’s hotel license goes through a hotel area by area. It splits music into two groups: “Recorded Music Activity” and “Live Entertainment Activity”. It leaves out a third group, “Third-Party Licensable Activity”, which it defines in three parts (ASCAP hotel license, 2022 form). The quotes below come from that form unless another source is named. Other PROs’ licenses, and later ASCAP versions, may use different words. - Lobby and background music : Recorded music is any public performance at the hotel “whether in common areas (including gyms and spas) or Lodging Rooms”. It can come from recordings, digital audio, radio or TV. The hotel license leaves out music from “any jukebox, background music service” when its public performance is “otherwise licensed or licensable”. That means licensed, or licensable, through ASCAP or the Jukebox License Office. SESAC adds a limit for background music services. Their license “only extends to the music they supply” to places with “no admission, membership or similar charge” (SESAC FAQ). - Restaurant and bar : If the hotel runs an outlet itself, the outlet is part of the premises the hotel license covers. Some areas are run, or mainly controlled

ASCAP’s 2022 hotel form sets two fees. The recorded music fee for each hotel follows its number of guest rooms (“Lodging Rooms”). The live entertainment fee follows what the hotels spend on live entertainment in a year. The license covers only the hotels listed in its Schedule A. The licensee’s other hotels “are not covered by or subject to this License Agreement” (ASCAP hotel license, 2022 form). GMR says its rate depends on “your type of business and how the music is presented to the public” (Global Music Rights FAQ). SESAC says its fees “are determined by relevant industry criteria” (SESAC FAQ). To give a sense of scale, Bloomberg reported this example from the American Hotel & Lodging Association: “A large hotel that hosts occasional live music events could be paying a single PRO $5,000 to $20,000 a year. If it’s paying all of the major PROs, it could be incurring as much as $80,000 in fees, according to the association” (Bloomberg via Indianapolis Business Journal, July 9, 2025). That is the association’s example, not a price quote for any hotel. What does a music license cost? covers what drives fees for restaurants and bars.

h: Can my venue use popular songs in Instagram or TikTok videos?
t: Music in a video you post is a different use from music played in your room. The apps’ own terms set tighter limits on business and promo posts than on personal ones. Rules: United States Other countries On this page A different useWhat the platforms sayCommon optionsNext step

h: A different use from the music in your room
t: The licenses a venue holds for music on its premises are about performing music there. Take ASCAP’s hotel license as an example. It does not give the right to perform its music “to persons beyond the Premises by any means, methodology or technology”. That includes “internet-connected websites, software applications, systems, platforms”. It also gives no right to “reproduce, copy or distribute” the music, or to use the sound recordings (ASCAP Musical Works License Agreement for Hotels and Motels, 2022 form, published by AHLA). Putting a song into a video needs other rights. SESAC says it “does not represent the rights needed to reproduce a musical composition into a video”. It adds: “These rights are generally called sync rights”. In plain words, sync means setting music to pictures. SESAC also says that using an existing recording means contacting “the record label that owns said recording” (SESAC FAQ). For playing music in public, SESAC says “Many major social media platforms are already licensed with SESAC”. It says it does not usually license “individual users’ channels or pages” (SESAC FAQ). The radio and TV exemption for small venues does not help here either. It never covers

h: What the platforms’ own terms say
t: Each platform sets its own rules for music in its app. These are the platforms’ words about their own services. They are not a statement of the law. - Facebook and Instagram (Meta) : Meta’s Music Guidelines apply “if you post, share, or promote any videos or other content containing music on any Meta Products”. Meta Products include Instagram (Meta Products). The guidelines say: “Use of music for commercial or non-personal purposes in particular is prohibited unless you have obtained appropriate licenses”. They also say: “Nothing in these terms constitutes any authorization by us with respect to any use of music” (Meta Music Guidelines, effective March 26, 2024). - Instagram’s music library : Instagram says: “The music available in our library is intended for personal, non-commercial use”. It adds that “certain business accounts and certain types of posts do not have access to the library” (Instagram Help, access to the licensed music library). A reel you boost as an ad “can’t use licensed music”. Instead, Instagram recommends “royalty-free music, like what’s available in our Sound Collection, or original audio” (Instagram Help, how to boost a reel). - TikTok : TikTok’s Commercial

This is general information, not a recommendation for any post. Each option has its own terms. - The platform’s commercial library. Instagram says Meta’s Sound Collection has “over 14,000 songs and sounds”. It says they “can be used for commercial purposes like ads” (Instagram Help). TikTok’s Commercial Music Library stays on TikTok: “Commercial Uses outside of TikTok are not permitted and no rights are granted by TikTok for such uses” (TikTok CML terms). A track you pick in one app may not cover the same video posted somewhere else. - Music licensed for video. For sync rights to a specific song, SESAC points to the song’s publishers. h: What happens if a restaurant or bar plays music without a license?
t: Usually letters and calls come first. Sometimes a federal lawsuit follows. Here is what the PROs and the law say, step by step. Rules: United States Other countries On this page How it unfoldsWhat the law allowsWho may be held responsibleWhat to do

Copyright law gives the owner of a song the exclusive right “to perform the copyrighted work publicly” (17 U.S.C. §106(4)). Playing music for the public, such as in a bar, is a public performance. Groups called performing rights organizations (PROs) license that right to businesses. ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR are PROs. They do this for songwriters and publishers. The PROs’ own words point to a slow, step-by-step path: - Letters and calls. ASCAP says it will sue when a bar or club owner refuses a license. It adds, “but this only happens after many attempts to educate them about their obligations under Federal law” (ASCAP, why ASCAP licenses bars, restaurants and music venues). A BMI spokesperson told Bloomberg that lawsuits are “always a last resort”. The spokesperson added that BMI “spends sometimes years on educational outreach” (Bloomberg via Indianapolis Business Journal, July 9, 2025). - A visit. BMI said in the same report that if those efforts are ignored, “an in-person visit might occur, and BMI may take legal action” (Bloomberg via IBJ). - A lawsuit in federal court. Federal district courts hear copyright cases. The law says “No State court shall have jurisdiction” over them

Federal copyright law says what a court may order if it finds infringement. Infringement means using someone’s work in a way that breaks their copyright. The quotes below come straight from the law. - Damages, two ways : An infringer is liable for one of two amounts. The first is the copyright owner’s “actual damages and any additional profits of the infringer”. In plain words, that is what the owner lost, plus any extra profit the infringer made. The second is statutory damages (17 U.S.C. §504(a)). The copyright owner may choose statutory damages “at any time before final judgment is rendered” (§504(c)(1)). - Statutory damages per work : US law sets statutory damages at “Not less than $750 or more than $30,000 as the court considers just”, for each work infringed (17 U.S.C. §504(c)(1)). Here, a work means one song. - If the infringement was willful : The copyright owner has to prove that the infringement was committed willfully. The court has to find so too. Then the court “may increase the award of statutory damages to a sum of not more than $150,000” per work (§504(c)(2)). - If the infringement was innocent : The infringer has to prove that it “was not aware and had no reason to

The PROs say the business is responsible, not only the DJ or the band. ASCAP says: “Anyone involved in enabling an unlicensed public performance may be held liable for copyright infringement, including corporate officers, business owners and managers” (ASCAP Music Licensing FAQs). ASCAP also says that “all who participate in, or are responsible for, performances of music are legally responsible”. It adds that “it is the business owner who obtains the license” (ASCAP, why ASCAP licenses bars, restaurants and music venues). SESAC says “a business cannot shift its responsibility to musicians or entertainers” (SESAC, “Who is responsible for paying music licensing fees?”). In short, the PROs say the business owner must get the license. These statements give the PROs’ own view. How this applies to one venue or person is a question for a licensed attorney. Do I need a license for live music, DJs or karaoke? covers performers in more detail.

h: Holiday songs follow the same rules
t: Copyright law gives the owner of a song the sole right “to perform the copyrighted work publicly” (17 U.S.C. §106(4)). Playing a song in public is called a public performance. The law says a song is played “publicly” when it is played “at a place open to the public”. It is also played publicly “at any place where a substantial number of persons outside of a normal circle of a family and its social acquaintances is gathered” (17 U.S.C. §101, definitions). In short: a place open to the public, or a place where many people beyond family and friends get together. Neither section has special rules for holiday music. Many of the most famous holiday songs are new enough to still be under copyright. ASCAP made a 2025 chart of its 25 most-played holiday songs. It says ASCAP songwriters and composers wrote, co-wrote or arranged all of them. The list includes “Sleigh Ride” (1948), “Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer” (1949), “White Christmas” (1941) and “All I Want for Christmas Is You” (1994) (ASCAP’s 2025 holiday charts, as reported by BroadwayWorld, December 11, 2025). h: Old carols: the song, the arrangement, the recording
t: Copyright on old works does run out. When it ends, the work is in the public domain. The U.S. Copyright Office says that “all works published in the United States before January 1, 1931, are in the public domain” (U.S. Copyright Office, Circular 15A, revised April 2026). Works published in 1930 entered the public domain on January 1, 2026 (Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain, Public Domain Day 2026). But the Office warns that “there are a number of exceptions” to this general rule. In many cases, it says, you should ask a copyright attorney before you decide if a work is still under copyright (U.S. Copyright Office, Circular 22, How to Investigate the Copyright Status of a Work, revised April 2026). A venue rarely plays the bare carol. It plays one arrangement of it, in one recording. Each of these layers is looked at on its own: - The song : The words and music, as they were first published. Because Google's authorization semantics apply across the relevant Sereinora Google project, using this control revokes Sereinora's YouTube authorization for both publishing and read/Analytics functionality. On successful revocation, Sereinora removes the applicable locally stored OAuth credentials and Authorized Data in accordance with YouTube's requirements. You may also revoke access independently through Google's account security and third-party access settings. Revoking Sereinora's authorization or deleting locally stored Sereinora data does not delete videos or other content stored by YouTube. Content hosted on YouTube must be managed separately through YouTube or another appropriately authorized client.
